title: F to H --- Why the H Says Nothing

lessons.title: f becomes h — why the h says nothing
lessons.gloss: the law that explains why the Spanish h is silent — it is standing where an f used to be

segments.text: Since your first chapter you have known that the Spanish h is silent. You were told it as a fact. Here is the reason, and it turns the fact into a tool.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: a letter standing on a grave

segments.text: Where Spanish has a silent h-, Latin very often had an f-.
You already hold the proof. Hablar comes from Latin fabulārī — and English took the same root and kept the f: fable, fabulous.

The sound did not vanish overnight. Latin f- weakened to a breathy h, the breath faded, and eventually nothing was left — but the spelling had already settled, so Spanish went on writing a letter it had stopped saying. The silent h is a gravestone. It marks where a sound used to be.
Which makes it a decoder. Meet an unfamiliar Spanish word beginning with h-, put an f back, and look for the English:

utterances: Spanish: hijo. put the f back: fijo from fīlium. English friend: filial, affiliate.
Spanish: hierro. put the f back: fierro from ferrum. English friend: ferrous, ferric.
Spanish: harina. put the f back: farina. English friend: farinaceous.
Spanish: higo. put the f back: figo from fīcus. English friend: fig.
Spanish: hoja. put the f back: foja from folia. English friend: foliage, portfolio.

segments.text: Not one of those five words has been taught in this book, and you can read all five.
Two honest limits, because a decoder you trust too far will mislead you.
Not every h is a dead f. Hola is not, and hasta came from Arabic.
And not every Latin f became h. Fácil, fuerte and forma kept theirs; the change left f alone before ue and r.
So this is a lead, not a guarantee. Put the f back and believe it when an English word appears.

segments.prompt: Why is the Spanish h silent?
acceptedResponses: it marks where an f used to be
the f weakened to h and then to nothing

feedback.incorrect: Latin f- weakened to a breath and then to nothing; the spelling stayed.

segments.prompt: Which English word is hablar's friend, once you put the f back?

feedback.correct: Hablar and fable are the same root.
feedback.incorrect: Fable — from fabulari, to tell tales.

segments.prompt: You meet hierro and have never seen it. Decode it.

feedback.incorrect: Put the f back: fierro, ferrum. Iron, as in ferrous.

segments.prompt: Is every Spanish h a dead f?
acceptedResponses: no — hola and hasta are not

feedback.incorrect: No. Hola is not, and hasta came from Arabic.

segments.text: Why is the h silent? (It stands where an f used to be.) What do you do with an unfamiliar h- word? (Put the f back and look for the English.) Is it always right? (No — a lead, not a guarantee.)
